{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-mn-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"0f09e99667bd10b7262e2183c093260a8ee3c656912eed5d4d0fceee4d7a981b","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-mn-class-d:lineage:19","source_registry_sha256":"960e2daa314aff60b32f5124e42324d79615ce2a3ea953a336216b4593c0c910","source_liveness_sha256":"0b70283fc58b1f8ea1822994a92e3ce7ff4b722004376a9cd819180969b6fe1e"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Traffic laws: speed, signaling, lanes, turns, roundabouts, J-turns, U-turns and passing","heading":"C — Traffic laws part one: keeping right, speed limits and fines, signaling, lanes and blind spots, turns and turns on red, roundabouts, J-turns and divided highways, U-turns, right-lane travel, passing and backing","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Traffic laws part one: keeping right, speed limits and fines, signaling, lanes and blind spots, turns and turns on red, roundabouts, J-turns and divided highways, U-turns, right-lane travel, passing and backing
Knowledge domain: how Minnesota law expects you to position, pace and steer your vehicle on public roads, from the keep-right rule and the speed limits through signaling, lane changes, turns, roundabouts, J-turns, U-turns, passing and backing.

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Minnesota's traffic laws cover every person who drives on a public road anywhere in the state. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
On roads of sufficient width you keep to the right side unless you are passing a vehicle going your way, the right side is closed for construction or repair, the road has three marked lanes, signs make it one-way, or you are moving over for a stopped authorized vehicle under the Move Over Law. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
Under the basic speed law your speed must be reasonable for the current weather, traffic and road conditions, and the posted limit is the highest speed allowed on that road. [A01]
Why it matters: a speed under the posted limit can still be illegal when conditions are poor.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
Where a minimum speed limit is posted, driving below it under normal conditions is illegal. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit in an alley under ideal conditions is 10 mph. [A01]
Why it matters: the alley limit is a classic numeric item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit on urban or town roads under ideal conditions is 30 mph. [A01]
Why it matters: the town road limit is a classic numeric item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
Unless signs say otherwise, the speed limit under ideal conditions is 55 mph in every location not otherwise listed. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A01
In a school zone you must slow down when children are present, and in a work or construction zone you must slow down and drive carefully. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0029]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A02
Speeding can bring a fine, and extra fines apply when you drive 20 mph or more above the posted limit. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A02
Driving faster than 100 mph leads to revocation of your driving privileges for at least six months. [A02]
Why it matters: the revocation trigger and its minimum length are likely test items.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A02
You must slow down when approaching or passing a stopped emergency vehicle with flashing emergency lights, and breaking this rule adds a surcharge of at least $25 to the speeding fine. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
Watch for flag persons, pedestrians, barricades, flares or reflectors in the roadway and reduce speed for them, as well as in bad weather and on poor road surfaces. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
Reduce speed on narrow or winding roads and as you near a curve, the top of a hill or a railroad crossing. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
On gravel or dirt roads slow down, because stopping takes longer and the vehicle skids more easily in a turn. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
Bridges may carry their own speed limits and No Passing signs, and you must watch for and obey them. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
Turn on your signal at least 100 feet before you turn, and keep it on until the turn or lane change is finished. [A02]
Why it matters: the signaling distance is one of the most tested numbers in this chapter.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
In daylight you may use hand and arm signals along with or in place of turn signals, but not at night or in a vehicle that hides your hand from other drivers. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A02
A traffic lane exists whether or not it is marked, and you must stay inside one lane without weaving or straddling the markings. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0030]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A03
Before changing lanes make sure there is room beside, behind and ahead of you, and turn your head to check the new lane instead of relying only on mirrors. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A03
Blind spots are areas your mirrors cannot show; the vehicle's design and roof pillars decide where they are, and a dirty windshield or glare can add temporary ones. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A03
While you wait to turn, keep the wheels pointed straight and your foot on the brake so a rear-end hit is less likely to shove you into oncoming traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A03
When waiting to turn left on a green light with traffic coming toward you, pull into the intersection until your body lines up with the curb line, and you may only get to turn once the light turns yellow. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A03
Many intersections allow a right turn on red after a complete stop in the correct lane, unless a No Turn on Red sign is posted, and only after checking every direction for pedestrians and traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A03
A left turn on red is allowed in certain cases only when turning from a one-way street onto another one-way street, after a complete stop and once the intersection is clear. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A04
For a left turn, check behind you and signal, move into the lane nearest the center line, or just right of the road's center if lanes are unmarked, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the first lane to the right of the center line. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A04
For a right turn, check behind you and signal, move close to the right curb, look both ways, yield if needed, and finish in the lane next to the curb. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A05
Where signs or lane markings show two or more turning lanes, stay in your own lane all the way through the turn. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A05
As you approach a roundabout, slow down, pick your lane before entering if it has more than one lane, yield to pedestrians and bicyclists crossing, and watch for signs or markings that require or forbid certain moves. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A05
Enter a roundabout only after yielding to vehicles already circulating and after all traffic coming from your left has cleared. [A05]
Why it matters: yielding to traffic already inside is the core roundabout rule.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A05
Inside a roundabout drive counterclockwise to your exit and never stop, pass or change lanes. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A05
If an emergency vehicle approaches while you are in a roundabout, leave the roundabout right away and then pull over. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A05
Any combination vehicle, or a vehicle over 40 feet long or more than 10 feet wide, may leave its lane as needed to get through a roundabout while watching other traffic. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A06
J-turns exist to cut deaths and injuries from broadside crashes on four-lane divided highways. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A06
At a J-turn every side-street driver turns right; to cross or go left you stop completely, turn right onto the highway, move into the marked left-turn lane at the median opening and make a U-turn. [A06]
Why it matters: the J-turn sequence is a Minnesota-specific procedure.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A06
When finishing the U-turn at a J-turn you must yield to oncoming traffic, stopping if needed, before entering the through lanes. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0035]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A07
U-turns are banned on interstate freeways, and also near hilltops or on curves where drivers coming toward you could not see you from 1,000 feet away. [A07]
Why it matters: the U-turn sight distance is easy to confuse with the passing sight distance.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A07
On highways with more than one lane in your direction, use the right-hand lane when one is available, and leave the left-most lane to let another vehicle pass when practical. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0036]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A08
After passing you must be back on the right side of the road before you come within 100 feet of an oncoming vehicle. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A08
You may not pass where a No Passing Zone sign is posted or where a solid yellow line is on your side of the center line, and double solid yellow lines forbid passing in both directions. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A08
Never pass on a hill or curve unless you can clearly see at least 700 feet of road ahead. [A08]
Why it matters: the passing sight distance is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A08
Passing is not allowed within 100 feet of an intersection, an underpass, a tunnel or a railroad crossing. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A08
You may pass on the right only when it is safe and the vehicle ahead is turning or about to turn left, or the road has room for two or more lanes of moving traffic each way, or it is a one-way road wide enough for two or more lanes with nothing in the way. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

FACT_ID: sec05-F43 | anchor: A08
Backing up on freeways or expressways is not allowed except for emergency vehicles on duty, and backing on public roads can lead to a reckless or careless driving charge. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0037]

Misconceptions: driving at the posted limit is not always legal, because the basic speed law also requires a speed reasonable for conditions; a right turn on red is not allowed where a No Turn on Red sign is posted; left on red is not allowed from a two-way street; cars already in a roundabout have the right-of-way over entering cars; you may not pass on the right by using the shoulder or a bike lane.
Mnemonics: alley ten, town thirty, everywhere else fifty-five; signal a hundred feet ahead and be back in your lane a hundred feet before an oncoming car; see seven hundred feet to pass, be seen from a thousand feet to U-turn; in a roundabout yield, go counterclockwise and do not stop.
Glossary: basic speed law means the rule that speed must suit current conditions; blind spot means an area around the vehicle the mirrors cannot show; roundabout means a circular intersection where traffic flows counterclockwise around a centre island; J-turn means a right turn followed by a U-turn at a median opening used instead of crossing a divided highway; combination vehicle means a vehicle towing another unit.
